title: How the Browser Draws & CSS Layout

scenes.say: One line of JavaScript can freeze a whole page. You'll learn which line, and why. And you'll win any C S S argument about which rule applies.

lines.cue: win any C S S argument

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Follow a page from H T M L to pixels. Spot the loop that forces a thousand layouts. And size boxes, pick flex or grid, and win on specificity.
lines: Follow a page from HTML to pixels
Spot the loop that forces 1,000 layouts
Size boxes, pick flex or grid, win specificity

scenes.title: From text file to pixels
scenes.statement: The browser receives HTML and CSS as plain text. Name the steps that turn it into the pixels you see.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. The browser gets plain text. For example, one heading tag and one color rule. We want a red heading on screen. Which steps happen in between?

scenes.head: Think of building a house
scenes.say: Think of building a house. First, a blueprint says which rooms exist. Then paint swatches say how each room looks. Then you measure where every wall goes. Then you paint. The browser does these four jobs, in this order, for every page.

scenes.head: The real names
scenes.say: Now the real names. Parsing H T M L gives the D O M, a tree of nodes. Parsing C S S gives the C S S O M, a tree of rules. Merge them into the render tree. Layout sizes and places each box. Paint fills the pixels.

items.label: from CSS
items.cue: C S S O M, a tree

scenes.head: What a change re-runs
scenes.say: After the first render, a change re-runs the pipeline from some step onward. Change a width or a position, and the browser restarts at layout. That's a reflow, and a repaint follows. Change a color, and it skips layout. Just a repaint. Change only transform or opacity, and the graphics card composites. No layout, no repaint.
Your turn. You animate a box's top from zero to a hundred pixels. Sixty frames a second. Which steps run on every frame? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Animating `top` from 0 to 100px: what runs each frame?

scenes.head: Same slide, two costs
scenes.say: Layout, paint, and composite, on every frame. Top is a position, so each frame restarts at layout. Sixty reflows a second. The fix is transform. It only composites, so the same slide costs almost nothing. In the interview, say animate transform and opacity.

chapters.title: The loop that freezes a page

scenes.title: Why does this loop freeze the page?
scenes.statement: A script sets each item's width and reads its height, for 1,000 items. The page locks up. Make it fast.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, a thousand items: write, read, write, read. We want one layout, not a thousand.

scenes.head: A foreman with a notebook
scenes.say: Think of a foreman with a notebook. You change a wall's width. He jots it down. No measuring yet. Then you ask, how tall is that wall right now? He can't guess. He must stop and re-measure every wall. Reading a height is that question.

scenes.head: 1,000 passes, 1,000 layouts
scenes.say: In the browser the notebook is a flag: layout is stale. A write sets the flag, which is free. A read of offset height needs a true answer, so the browser runs layout now. Write, read, write, read: that's a thousand layouts. Read everything first, then write everything. Layout runs once.

scenes.head: Read first, write second
scenes.say: Here it is in code. On the left, slow. Each pass writes a width, then reads offset height, so every pass forces layout. On the right, fast. Read every height into a list first. Then write every width. One layout.

panels.label: bad
good

scenes.say: Your turn. A loop sets width, then color, on a thousand items. It never reads anything. How many layouts run? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Loop sets `width` and `color` on 1,000 items. No reads. Layouts?

scenes.head: Layouts per run
scenes.say: One, at the end of the frame. Writes alone only mark things stale, so the browser lays out once, just before painting. The mixed loop: a thousand. Batched, reads then writes: one again. Same work, a thousand times the layouts.

scenes.head: Reads that look harmless
scenes.say: Careful, many reads look harmless. Offset height forces layout. So does get bounding client rect. And scroll top. Plain style writes only mark things stale.

scenes.title: How wide is this card?
scenes.statement: A card is 200px wide with 20px of padding and a 2px border on every side. How wide is it on screen?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, a card two hundred wide, with padding and border. On screen? Not two hundred.

scenes.head: A gift in a box
scenes.say: Think of a gift in a box. The gift is the content, two hundred pixels wide. Around it, bubble wrap: padding. Then the box wall: the border. The gap to the next box is the margin. It never counts.

scenes.head: Adding it up
scenes.say: Add it up. Content: two hundred. Padding is twenty on the left and twenty on the right: forty. The border is two on each side: four. Total, two hundred forty four. By default, width means content only.

scenes.head: `box-sizing` changes the rule
scenes.say: Set box sizing to border box, and width now includes padding and border. The card stays two hundred, and the content shrinks to make room. Most projects set this once, for everything.
Your turn. Default sizing. Width three hundred, padding ten on each side, border five on each side. How wide on screen? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Same sum, new numbers
scenes.say: Three hundred thirty. Content three hundred. Padding twenty in total. Border ten in total. Add them up and the box is three thirty wide.

scenes.head: Two 50% columns that overflow
scenes.say: Here's the bug this causes. Two columns, each fifty percent of a thousand pixels. Each has padding. Default sizing makes each five forty, so they spill over. Border box makes each five hundred, and they fit.

scenes.title: Lay out a nav bar and a gallery
scenes.statement: A nav bar needs a logo on the left and a menu on the right. A gallery needs three equal columns. Which tool for each?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A nav bar and a card gallery. For example, a logo and a menu, and four cards. We want to pick the right layout tool for each.

scenes.head: A shelf and an egg carton
scenes.say: Think of two ways to store things. A shelf: items in one line. That is flexbox, one axis. An egg carton: fixed slots in rows and columns together. That is grid, two axes.

scenes.head: Flex puts items on one line
scenes.say: Here is a flex container, a box a thousand pixels wide. Three items, each a hundred pixels. Display flex lines them up on one axis, packed at the start. The empty space is leftover.
Your turn. Now add justify content space between. First item at the left edge, last at the right edge. How wide is each gap between items? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Flex puts items on one line
scenes.say: Three fifty. Seven hundred pixels free, split in two gaps. B slides to the middle. C slides to the right edge.

scenes.head: Grid fills rows and columns
scenes.say: Now grid. Three equal columns with a gap. Four cards fill the slots in order. The fourth does not fit in the first row, so it wraps to a second row by itself.

scenes.head: Nav, gallery, and centering
scenes.say: In C S S, the nav is display flex with space between. The gallery is display grid, three equal columns, sixteen pixels of gap. And to center anything, make its parent flex, and center both axes. Flex when content decides, grid when the layout decides.

scenes.title: Which color wins?
scenes.statement: Two rules match the same heading. One uses an id. The other chains three classes. Which color shows?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. Two rules hit one heading. For example, an id says red, three chained classes say blue. The answer is red. Let's see why.

scenes.head: Specificity is a medal table
scenes.say: Think of an Olympic medal table. Compare gold first. Only on a tie, silver. Only then bronze. Same for selectors: ids, classes, elements. Three silvers never beat one gold.

scenes.head: Score each selector
scenes.say: Score each rule. The id hero scores one, zero, zero. The chain of three classes scores zero, three, zero. Compare left to right. The first slot is one against zero, so the id wins. We never even count the three.

scenes.head: Prove it in the browser
scenes.say: Here is the page. A heading with id hero and classes a, b, and c. Three rules: the id says red, the classes say blue, the element says green. The heading renders red.
Your turn. Two rules, one list item with class on. First rule: class menu, then class on, red. Second rule: list, item, class on, blue. Which color? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `.menu .on` red, then `ul li.on` blue. Which wins?

scenes.head: Score both rules
scenes.say: Red. Menu on scores zero, two, zero. List item on scores zero, one, two. The middle slot decides: two beats one. File order never mattered.

scenes.head: Ties, inline and `!important`
scenes.say: Same score? The later rule wins. Inline style beats any selector. Important beats inline, so it is a last resort. Instead, lower the selector.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does a browser render? Parse into trees, then layout, paint, composite. Reflow versus repaint? Reflow recomputes positions, so it costs more. Why is transform cheap? It only composites. Common mistake? Reading offset height between writes.

it only composites: no layout, no repaint

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Box model? Content, padding, border, margin. Use border box so width includes padding. Flex or grid? Flex for one axis, grid for two. Center a div? Flex, then center both axes. A stubborn style? Lower the selector, avoid important.
rows: flex: one axis. grid: two axes

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Try these next. Open the DevTools Performance tab, record the thousand item loop, and find the layout bars. Animate a box with top, then with transform, and compare. Then rebuild a nav, a gallery, and the specificity quiz by hand.

scenes.say: So say this. The browser builds the D O M and C S S O M, then layout, paint, composite. Reads between writes force layout, so batch them. And border box, flex or grid, and specificity decide your layout.

Batch reads before writes: one layout, not 1,000.
`border-box`; flex for 1D, grid for 2D; ids beat classes.
